title: Design a URL shortener
summary: Plan a service that turns a long web address into a short link. Handle code collisions, redirects, expired links, and unsafe destinations.
introduction: A short link is like a small label on a large folder. The label helps us find the stored destination, but it is not the destination itself. We will design a service that saves and looks up these labels.
learningObjectives: Map a short code to a checked destination
Explain unique codes and safe collision handling
Plan redirects, expiry, caching, and abuse controls

blocks.text: The service creates a short link and redirects visitors to its destination. For practice, assume 100 new links each day and many more opens than creates. Custom labels and detailed visitor tracking can wait.
A **redirect** is a reply telling the browser to visit another address. The short-link service looks up a record; it does not need to download the destination page itself.

blocks.alt: A browser opens a short code. The redirect service finds its link record, checks the destination and expiry, and returns a redirect.
blocks.caption: This shows reading an existing link. Creating a code also needs a unique-code check and clear rules for allowed destinations.

blocks.code:
Short-link design
POST /links {destination} -> {code, shortUrl}
GET /s/{code} -> temporary redirect or not-found reply

Link record
code: unique short label
destination: checked HTTP or HTTPS web address
createdAt, expiresAt, disabledAt

Create
Check address and creation limits.
Generate an unpredictable candidate code.
Insert only if the code is unused; retry a bounded number of collisions.

Open
Look up the code.
Check disabled/expired state.
Reply with HTTP 302 and the checked destination.
Unknown, expired, or disabled code -> clear unavailable page.
blocks.title: Worked design plan
blocks.caption: Read this as a design plan. It is not a running server or an API you can call.

blocks.text: Follow a link from creation to opening

items: A caller submits a destination. Use a URL parser, allow only intended schemes such as HTTPS, and limit the address length. A scheme is the part before the colon, such as https.
Generate an unpredictable code and try to insert it with a database uniqueness rule. A collision means the code is already used; generate another and retry within a set limit.
Return the new short link only after its record is saved. The code becomes an exact lookup key.
A visitor opens the short link. Look up the record, check its current state, then redirect or show a clear unavailable page.

blocks.text: Use storage and caching for the actual workload
One database table is a sensible start. A unique index on code both helps lookup and protects the code rule. A random generator alone cannot promise that two codes will never match.

Popular public links may be cached because reads are frequent. Give cache entries a short lifetime and clear them when a link is disabled. If a blocked link must stop immediately, check an up-to-date block decision before redirecting.

HTTP 302 is a temporary redirect in this plan. Set deliberate cache rules because destinations may expire or be disabled. A long-lived permanent redirect can remain in browsers after the service changes its mind.
When a lookup store is unavailable, a cache miss is a service failure, not proof that the code does not exist. A not-found reply is for a successful lookup that found no usable record.
An unpredictable code is not permission to read a private file. If a destination is private, its own service must check access. Anyone who sees a public short link may share it.

Short links can hide harmful destinations. Limit creation, provide a way to report abuse, and apply destination policies. A school-only service might allow only approved school domains. Valid URL syntax alone does not prove a destination is safe.
Avoid fetching destination pages merely to redirect. If a later preview feature fetches URLs, it needs separate rules against reaching private network addresses and other unintended targets.

items: Two creation requests generate the same candidate code. What should happen to the second insert?
The database rejects the duplicate code. The second request tries a new code within its retry limit; it must not replace the first destination.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not check that a code is unused and then assume it stays unused. Concurrent requests need a database uniqueness rule at insertion.
